title: It’s because…
description: This is the reason something happened.
details:
Example: It’s because the trains aren’t running.

Usage: Use to answer a why question or explain a situation.

title: That’s why…
description: This explains the result I’m talking about.
details:
Example: I missed the bus. That’s why I’m late.

Usage: Give the reason first, then the result after that’s why.

title: The thing is…
description: Here is the important point or difficulty.
details:
Example: I’d love to come. The thing is, I’m working.

Usage: Conversational; useful before explaining a complication.

title: To be honest…
description: I’m going to say what I really think or feel.
details:
Example: To be honest, I’d prefer to wait.

Usage: Useful before a frank explanation or preference; it can sound critical if your tone is harsh.

title: What I mean is…
description: This is the idea I’m trying to communicate.
details:
Example: What I mean is, we don’t have to decide today.

Usage: Useful when someone hasn’t understood your first explanation.

title: For example
description: Here is one case that shows what I mean.
details:
Example: We could cook something simple, for example, pasta.

Usage: Use to make a general suggestion or explanation more specific.

title: It depends on…
description: The answer changes according to this factor.
details:
Example: It depends on how much it costs.

Usage: Follow with a noun or a question clause: depends on the weather.

title: The main reason is…
description: This is the most important explanation.
details:
Example: The main reason is that it’s closer to work.

Usage: Use a noun or a clause beginning with that.

title: The problem is…
description: This is the difficulty we need to consider.
details:
Example: The problem is, we don’t have enough time.

Usage: Useful before explaining what prevents a plan from working.

title: So basically…
description: Here is the simple version of the explanation.
details:
Example: So basically, we need to book before Friday.

Usage: Conversational; summarise the key point without too many details.

title: In other words
description: I’ll express the same idea in a different way.
details:
Example: It’s optional. In other words, you don’t have to go.

Usage: Use to make a word or statement clearer.

title: Even if…
description: This condition would not change the result.
details:
Example: Even if it rains, I’m still going.

Usage: Use for a possibility; even though introduces a fact.

title: As long as…
description: This is okay if this condition is met.
details:
Example: We can go as long as we’re back by six.

Usage: Here it means provided that, rather than a length of time.

title: Otherwise…
description: This will happen if we don’t do that.
details:
Example: We need to leave now. Otherwise, we’ll be late.

Usage: Useful for explaining why an action is necessary.

title: It doesn’t mean…
description: That is not the conclusion you should draw.
details:
Example: It’s expensive, but it doesn’t mean it’s better.

Usage: Use to question an assumption about what something shows.

title: That makes sense
description: I understand the reason or logic.
details:
Example: You live nearby? That makes sense, then.

Usage: Acknowledges an explanation; it needn’t mean you agree with every detail.

title: I see what you mean
description: I understand the point you’re making.
details:
Example: I see what you mean. That would take longer.

Usage: Useful for acknowledging someone’s explanation or concern.

title: There’s more to it
description: The situation is more complicated than it seems.
details:
Example: It’s not just about money. There’s more to it.

Usage: Follow with the missing explanation when you can.

title: It’s not just…
description: There is another important factor as well.
details:
Example: It’s not just the price. It’s the travel time too.

Usage: Often followed by a second sentence explaining the other factor.

title: That said…
description: I want to add a point that balances what I said.
details:
Example: It’s expensive. That said, we’d use it every day.

Usage: Use for a qualification or a different side of the issue.
